books.section: Great Depression and the New Deal (1929-1939)

primary_sources: Herbert Hoover, address accepting the Republican presidential nomination, August 11, 1928

stimulus.text: “We in America today are nearer to the final triumph over poverty than ever before in the history of any land. The poorhouse is vanishing from among us. We have not yet reached the goal, but, given a chance to go forward with the policies of the last 8 years, we shall soon with the help of God be in sight of the day when poverty will be banished from this Nation.” — Herbert Hoover, speech accepting the Republican presidential nomination, August 11, 1928. Abridged.
stimulus.source_note: Herbert Hoover, address accepting the Republican presidential nomination, Stanford, California, August 11, 1928. Verbatim excerpt, abridged; public domain.

stem: A historian using Hoover's statement as evidence about 1928 would most need to consider that

options.text: Hoover spoke as a candidate in a boom year
Hoover had already served four years as president
options.misconception: Hoover had not served as president at all in 1928. He took office in March 1929, after winning this election.

options.text: the speech was written by Coolidge's advisers
options.misconception: There is no evidence Coolidge's advisers wrote Hoover's acceptance speech. Hoover was the nominee, speaking for himself.

options.text: poverty had already been abolished in the United States
options.misconception: Poverty had not been abolished. Hoover said the country was near the triumph over poverty, not that it had arrived.

rationales.A: Hoover was accepting his party's nomination in 1928, a boom year, so the statement is a campaign promise shaped by prosperity and by the need to praise the past 8 years.
rationales.B: Background from the books: Hoover was Secretary of Commerce before 1929 and became president in March 1929, so in August 1928 he had served no years as president.
rationales.C: The passage gives no reason to doubt Hoover's authorship, and a historian needs evidence, not a guess, to claim someone else wrote it.
rationales.D: Hoover himself says the goal is not yet reached: 'We have not yet reached the goal.'
rationales.general:
1. Ask who is speaking: Hoover, accepting a nomination.
2. Ask when: August 1928, a boom year before the crash.
3. Ask what that means: a candidate praises the past and promises more of it.
4. A historian must weigh that the statement is a campaign promise from a boom year.
Remember: always ask who is speaking and when, since a campaign speech is written to win votes.
